pairings.name: A · Bricolage Grotesque + Figtree
pairings.display: Bricolage Grotesque (variable, wght 200-800 + opsz 12-96, OFL-1.1, 76,888 bytes)
pairings.body: Figtree (variable, wght 300-900, OFL-1.1; normal 20,156 bytes + optional italic 20,928 bytes)
pairings.why: Warm, slightly quirky grotesque headings over a clean, friendly geometric sans. Reads like modern science-museum signage: precise but not cold, and the display face has enough character to carry the arcade game without a third font. Weakness: both families have proportional figures by default, so numeric readouts must set font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums (measured in Chrome: works in both).

pairings.name: B · Fraunces + Source Sans 3
pairings.body: Source Sans 3 (variable, wght 200-900, OFL-1.1; normal 28,872 bytes + optional italic 28,460 bytes)
pairings.why: Editorial and humane: a soft old-style serif over a neutral humanist sans, like a well-made science magazine. The most elegant of the three. Weaknesses: Fraunces hairlines get thin on the dark background (keep weight 500 or more), the mood is bookish rather than playful so the arcade game fits less well, and Fraunces has no tabular figures in this file, so all readouts must use Source Sans 3 (tabular by default, measured).

pairings.name: C · Oxanium + IBM Plex Sans
pairings.body: IBM Plex Sans (variable, wght 100-700, OFL-1.1; normal 45,712 bytes + optional italic 50,184 bytes)
pairings.why: Instrument-console look: squared, chamfered headings like a scanner control panel over an engineered technical sans. Best numerals of the three (both families tabular by default, measured) and the best fit for the game. Weaknesses: closest to the sci-fi/gaming cliche the brief wants to avoid (a more readable cousin of Orbitron), least friendly for a general audience, and long headings feel mechanical.

result.recommendation:
Ship pairing A (Bricolage Grotesque + Figtree): it is the only one that is both friendly and precise, and its three files total 117,972 bytes (97,044 without the optional italic) against the 250 KB budget. Set font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums on every numeric readout. B is the runner-up if a more editorial tone is wanted. C is best kept for the game HUD only: Oxanium alone is 14,044 bytes and could be added to A for score digits (132,016 bytes total).

What was checked: all six families report OFL-1.1, latin subset and a variable version in the Fontsource API. All nine woff2 files downloaded with HTTP 200 and start with "wOF2". URLs in fonts.json are pinned (5.3.0, or 5.3.1 for Source Sans 3) and byte-identical to @latest today. fonts.json parses with node. Specimens A, B and C were screenshotted and viewed; A's heading was lightened from 700 to 650 after the first pass, and B and C were re-shot without changes and not viewed again after the re-shot.

Things to know before building:
- Licence text: licenseUrl points to the LICENSE files in the fontsource/font-files GitHub repository. The jsdelivr path <id>@latest/LICENSE returns a proxy notice, not a licence. OFL requires shipping the licence text alongside the fonts.
- Extra-axis file names: latin-opsz-normal.woff2 is not listed by the fonts API; I found it by trying the URL. The Bricolage wght-only file is smaller (41,344 bytes) but loses the large optical size that makes the headings look good.
- Glyph coverage: only the latin subset was tested. Greek letters such as beta and gamma were not checked and may fall back to a system font.
- Minus sign: the specimens use the real minus sign (U+2212) in "-1000 HU"; it rendered in all three.
- No git commands were run, as the task rules required.

result.summary: The draft has 35 claims (all status "unverified") plus attenuation, transmission, Hounsfield, interaction and photon-pair tables, with every derived number computed by scripts/build_draft.js in the same scratch folder; water at 511 keV is confirmed at 0.096 per cm from NIST and three PET papers. Main corrections: effective beam energy at 120 kV is roughly 55 to 70 keV, not 60 to 70; spongy bone is about +100 to +300 HU in vertebrae, and I found no primary source for the draft's +300 to +400; Kinahan 1998 proposed a hybrid segmentation/scaling method, while bilinear scaling comes from Burger 2002 and Carney 2006; the IAEA Hounsfield formula divides by mu_water alone; blood, muscle, fat and liver ranges were widened or shifted because the IAEA table and measured patient data disagree. Additions: the first CT scanners used iterative reconstruction before filtered back-projection, Rayleigh scatter is a minor third interaction, and Compton scatter is still the most common interaction in bone at 70 keV (62 percent, against 30 percent photoelectric). Still doubtful: the 0.26 g/cm3 inflated-lung density could not be traced to a primary source I could open; log-log interpolation at 70 keV runs 0.2 to 1.8 percent above NIST XCOM's direct values (both are in the table, and thick-bone transmission is sensitive to it); "first iterative product in 2009" may be contradicted by a 2008 GE product I did not verify; several plain-language ranges (spongy bone upper end, liver lower end, "commonly 64 rows") are my own summaries and are flagged in the notes.

The draft has 37 claims (all status "unverified") and 5 tables, and the file parses; most draft figures held, including the 0.019 mSv/MBq FDG coefficient (3.5 to 7 mSv), the 60-minute uptake, the 194 cm uEXPLORER and the 11-hour decay figure (1.55%, recomputed in scripts/calc.js). I corrected five things: the "low-dose" CT adds about 3 to 9 mSv in national surveys, not 1 to 3; typical totals are 10 to 19 mSv, with 25 mSv only for older full-diagnostic-CT scans; the CT pass is "less than two minutes" and the PET pass about 15 to 30 minutes, since no source supports "under a minute" or 10 minutes; the visit is about 2 hours; and US volume is 2.2 million scans in 2019, not about 2 million. Still doubtful: no authoritative worldwide scanner total exists in any source I could open, the worldwide scan figure (about 7 million a year) is my own derivation from UNSCEAR's 40 million procedures times a 17% PET share, and the US numbers come from a paid IMV survey read through trade press and an undated UNSCEAR table. Several sources were read only as abstracts or fetch-tool summaries (the EXPLORER papers, the infection/inflammation guideline, the NRC page, and ICRP 106 via the guidelines that quote it), and breastfeeding advice differs between the US label (9 hours) and European guidance (12 hours, contact only), so the site should not give a single number.
